anchors.paper_title: Deep learning on brief interictal intracranial recordings can accurately characterize seizure onset zones
anchors.reason: Dataset README says it accompanies Sundrani et al. 2025 (Epilepsia, doi:10.1111/epi.18478), the study reporting these resting-state SEEG recordings from 78 patients for SOZ classification.

metadata.methods_description: Five minutes of awake, eyes-closed resting-state SEEG were recorded per patient, at least 4 hours from electroclinical seizure activity. Signals were converted to a bipolar montage of adjacent contacts and filtered with MATLAB filtfilt Butterworth passbands (1-59, 61-119, 121-150 Hz). Contacts were localized on post-implantation CT with CRAVE and assigned to Desikan-Killiany regions. SOZs were defined per region as regions containing any contact involved in the ictal onset of at least one seizure.

citation_details.title: Computational neuroelectrophysiology and artificial intelligence for drug-resistant epilepsy: recent advances, current challenges, and future directions
citation_details.author: Yalin Wang, Zibo Yan, Yuanchu Gong, Wentao Lin, Tiancheng Wang, Yaqing Liu, Yanming Han, Minqiang Yang, Minghui Liu, Wei Chen, Bin Hu
citation_details.abstract: Drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) affects approximately 30% of epilepsy patients, with surgical cure rates below 70%. This challenge drives a fundamental paradigm shift from localizing a discrete epileptogenic zone toward characterizing and modulating the dysfunctional brain networks that initiate and propagate seizures. This review critically synthesizes how computational neuroelectrophysiology and artificial intelligence (AI) converge to propel this shift. We chart the trajectory from quantifying local biomarkers, including high-frequency oscillations and excitation-inhibition balance metrics, to mapping the topological properties of epileptic networks through functional and effective connectivity. The integration of these network features with AI techniques, particularly spatiotemporal deep learning architectures, has demonstrated significant potential for enhancing both the localization of the epileptogenic network and the prediction of postoperative outcomes. citation_details.author: Sándor Beniczky, Birgit Frauscher, Fábio Augusto Nascimento, Shobi Sivathamboo, Catalina Alvarado‐Rojas, Michael R. Sperling, Samden D. Lhatoo, Philippe Ryvlin, Levin Kuhlmann
citation_details.abstract: Electroencephalography is the most commonly used diagnostic tool for epilepsy. However, interpreting electroencephalograms (EEGs) requires expertise that is not widely available. Advances in digital technology and wearables have enabled large-scale EEG recording, generating vast amounts of data that cannot be managed through traditional visual interpretation by experts. Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to augment human expertise and reduce workloads. The application of artificial neural networks in analysing clinical EEG recordings has led to major breakthroughs, bringing AI-based EEG interpretation closer to clinical implementation. In this Review, we summarise the most important research and development results in this field from a clinical perspective. citation_details.title: DREChanNet: Patient-Relative iEEG Model for Channel-Wise Epileptogenic Zone Localization
citation_details.author: Yuanchu Gong, Zibo Yan, Yibo Lyu, Chen Chen, Qiang Li, Yuanfeng Zhou, Minqiang Yang, Yalin Wang, Wei Chen, Bin Hu
citation_details.abstract: Accurate localization of the epileptogenic zone (EZ) is essential for presurgical evaluation of patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) provides direct recordings of seizure-related brain activity, yet identifying epileptogenic contacts remains challenging because background electrophysiological activity and electrode coverage vary substantially across patients. These differences complicate the interpretation of absolute signal measurements and highlight the need to account for patient-specific recording context. We propose a patient-relative (PR) plug-in that expresses physiological features or learned representations relative to the distribution of recorded channels within each patient. This label-free operation can be incorporated as an input transformation or a lightweight correction to an existing predictor.
